newsitem.title: USA: Versace murder suspect seen as vengeful, narcissist.
newsitem.headline: Versace murder suspect seen as vengeful, narcissist.

text.p: Andrew Cunanan, the prime suspect in the killings of Gianni Versace and at least four other men, blurs the lines between the usual categories applied to multiple murderers, experts in the field said on Friday.

They believe Cunanan began as a "spree killer" set off by a desire for vengeance against a known victim, then developed a taste for cruelty shared by serial killers, and finally is seeking the infamy perceived by mass murderers.
"We're talking about a really different sort of killer," said Ann Rule, the Seattle-based author of 15 books on the topic including "The Stranger Beside Me."
"He does not fall conveniently into slots created by those among us who study multiple killers."
Unlike serial killers such as Ted Bundy, John Wayne Gacy or Jeffrey Dahmer, Cunanan has killed people he has known well and, apparently, not for perverse sexual pleasure, Rule and other experts said.

Serial killers tend to remain unidentified until they are caught. They often kill with their hands, unlike Cunanan who allegedly shot three of his victims. Some serial killers -- such as the Zodiac Killer with roughly 60 victims, and the Green River Killer who murdered some 48 prostitutes -- are never identified.

Spree killers, a category previously applied to Cunanan, generally erupt suddenly and kill a person they know, then go on a rampage where they kill a person a day for a week or two. But Cunanan's suspected execution-style murder of Versace on Tuesday came two months after his previous suspected killing, moving him into the serial killer category.

If Cunanan plotted Versace's murder, he shares certain characteristics of some mass murderers, such as Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, who generally act on a perceived grudge and often harbour a death wish that they carry out against their victims.

"From our point of view, he's a monster, but from his point of view, he's a victim of injustice getting a measure of revenge," said Jack Levin, an author and director of The Programme for the Study of Violence at Northeastern University.

Cunanan may be similar to other spree killers like Florida's Christopher Wilder, who killed a beautiful model friend who spurned his marriage proposal, then set out across the country killing amateur models before being gunned down in New Hampshire.

Cunanan may also have developed a desire for infamy after the fourth murder of a cemetery worker -- a seeming murder of opportunity -- and join America's long list of criminal celebrities. The brutal mutilation and possible torture of Chicago tycoon Lee Miglin's body may be an indication of Cunanan's rage or taste for cruelty. Or Cunanan may have a list of targets like Versace who symbolised the rich, gay, celebrated lifestyle he aspired to, experts said.
Levin cited evidence of Cunanan's large debts and the loss of his lavish lifestyle as likely leading to resentment.
"Versace represented all those gay wealthy celebrities who had exploited Cunanan over the last few years when he was a male prostitute," Levin said. "I think gays are at great risk."

"He does seem to combine characteristics of all the different kind of monsters, which is what I think makes him so fascinating to people," said Harold Schechter, author of "The A to Z Encyclopaedia of Serial Killers" and "Possession".

"Killers like this feel this terrible sense of nothingness, and they try to compensate for it by killing someone of stature (like Versace). They want the ultimate power over someone with global power. I think there are mixed motives ... and he is getting some kind of megalomaniacal narcissistic pleasure," Schechter said.
"I think he really wants to die. That is often the psychology of the mass murderer," he added.
"He's histrionic, he wants to be in the spotlight. He wants to have everyone talking about him," Rule said.
"Certainly there's violence and lot of rage, but his mind is working well. I think he's pretty good at being bad," she said.
